analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts, including lower rates on capital gains and inheritances, permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on January 23, 2009 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the expiration dates that Congress wrote into the 2001 and 2003 tax-cut laws (EGTRRA and JGTRRA). That would make permanent the lower income tax rates from 2001 and the low rates on dividends and capital gains from 2003, and would extend other provisions including the estate tax repeal timeline. Every provision was scheduled to lapse after 2010, so making them permanent means the lower rates never go back up.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with the highest incomes gain the most: the 2001 law cut the top income tax rates, the 2003 law cut taxes on investment income, and making both permanent means those lower rates never expire. Large estates also gain, since the 2001 law contained a phased-down estate tax that was headed toward full repeal; keeping that on permanent law avoids the estate tax's scheduled return.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Title IX of the 2001 tax law, which contained its expiration dates, so the 2001 income tax rate cuts become permanent law.
Repeals the expiration provision of the 2003 tax law so the reduced tax rates on dividends and capital gains also become permanent.
Because the 2001 law included a scheduled phase-out of the estate tax, making it permanent also keeps the tax on very large inheritances at its lowest scheduled level.

analysis.who_pays: Future taxpayers. Permanently extending tax cuts that were scheduled to expire means the federal government collects less revenue every year indefinitely, which means more federal debt, higher interest payments, or eventually deeper cuts to government programs or higher taxes elsewhere to close the gap.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes permanent tax cuts that were designed to expire, converting temporary measures into permanent revenue loss on the federal books; the same provisions, when partially extended, were a major driver of projected deficits.

The provisions being made permanent are concentrated at the top: the bill singles out the lower rates on dividends and capital gains, income that goes disproportionately to the highest-earning households, and locks in the estate-tax phase-down that benefits the largest inheritances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a permanent, ongoing tax reduction that is heaviest for high-income households, investors, and large estates, and pays for it with larger deficits borne by future taxpayers. For a typical middle-income household the annual benefit is modest, while the fiscal cost compounds indefinitely. The honest weighing is that this is a transfer of wealth across both income groups and generations, with the largest gains at the very top.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 23, 2009 by Rep. Sam Graves with Rep. Gary G. Miller as an original cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and that is the last recorded action in its entire history.
Eleven House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did, and no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place.
Because the bill died, the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts kept their scheduled expirations under current law rather than becoming permanent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The tax cuts were not locked in permanently, so the scheduled expirations stood and the long-run revenue loss was not put on the books. That outcome favors future taxpayers and anyone counting on that revenue, while wealthier households and large estates lost the chance to make the lower rates permanent through this bill (though Congress later debated the same provisions separately).

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Future taxpayers; the cuts did not become permanent

for.name: Rep. Sam Graves
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent.

for.name: Rep. Gary G. Miller
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Charles Rangel (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans in a House controlled by 253 Democrats; the Democratic-run committee never moved the bill, and no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill makes permanent the 2001 top-rate cuts and the 2003 low rates on dividends and capital gains, income concentrated among the wealthiest households. The cost shows up as permanent federal revenue loss carried by everyone else.
The 2001 law phased down the estate tax on the largest inheritances; making that law permanent keeps the tax on multi-million-dollar estates at its lowest level indefinitely.
